title: He wrote poetry in the conqueror's language, and was sewn into a sack and thrown in the river
dek: Bashshar ibn Burd was the grandson of a slave and a blind poet who mocked Arabs in Arabic and insulted a caliph and lived twenty more years — until one poem put him in the Tigris.
why: Medium information density, but it strings together the political freedom of the eighth-century Abbasid dynasty, Persian nationalism and the golden age of Arabic poetry into a single line — suited to listeners interested in literary history and imperial politics.
who: Readers interested in Abbasid political history, Arabic poetry, or the predicament of writers on the margins of empire; anyone who wants to understand how literature survives between total power and tolerance.
skip: The panegyric analysis from 1:28:55 to 1:34:10 is fairly granular and can be skipped quickly.

points.h: Persians counterattacked the Arabs in the Arabs' own language
points.body: Bashshar ibn Burd was an early literary representative of the Shu'ubiyya movement. The word comes from "peoples" in Quran 49:13: "We made you into nations and tribes, that you may know one another." For Persian Muslims, if the scripture plainly said Muslims were equal, there was no reason to bow to Arab elites just because they were Arabs — Arab Muslims should not live in garrison cities lording it over other Muslims in the provinces. The movement was mainly started by Persians, but it also included other conquered peoples, and its demand was equal rights. Bashshar wrote poetry in the conqueror's language, but his origins left him sympathetic to the conquered.

points.h: His grandfather was a slave, his father a freedman
points.body: Bashshar was born in Basrah around 713. Two generations earlier, his grandfather had fought the Muslim conquerors in Tukharistan in the Oxus valley (today northern Afghanistan), was taken captive as a slave, and died in Basrah; his father was freed and joined an Arab tribe. Bashshar later told stories about how noble his paternal lineage was, but the episode states plainly that the truth of these stories is unknown. He was disfigured by smallpox in childhood, was blind, and was large and heavy of body. He himself said blindness actually helped him write poetry: "lack of sight strengthens the acuteness of the heart and cuts out interference from things which are visible."

points.h: He wrote poems mocking Arabs for eating lizards
points.body: In one satire, Bashshar declared that his grandfather and father were the noblest of Persians, that the Roman emperor was his uncle, and that they all wore crowns; his father wore Persian sable and drank from gold cups, never followed mangy camels singing camel songs, never dug up desert melons to stave off hunger, and never dug lizards out of stony ground to eat. The episode notes that this lineage was mostly invented, but the satirical intent is clear: Persia is the land of civilization, and the Arabs can keep their wretched qasidas that romanticize the dry desert. His attitude toward Bedouin poetry was playfully irreverent, and at the same time he could wield its conventions with complete fluency.

points.h: One poem put him in the Tigris
points.body: Bashshar had a tense relationship with the caliph al-Mahdi (r. 775-785), who once ordered him to stop writing love poetry; he ignored it. According to the historian al-Tabari, around 783 Bashshar wrote a poem saying: wake up, sons of Umayya, you have slept too long; the Persian bureaucrat Ya'qub b. Dawud is the caliph, your caliphate is ruined, go look for God's caliph among the tambourines and lutes. This amounted to saying the Abbasid dynasty could be replaced by the Umayyads they had usurped — crossing from insolence into sedition. He was imprisoned, beaten half to death, sewn into a sack and thrown into the Tigris to drown, at about seventy years old.

points.h: He insulted a caliph and lived twenty more years
points.body: In 762, descendants of the Prophet's daughter Fatima rose in revolt against the Abbasids in Medina; Bashshar sided with the rebels and wrote a poem telling the reigning caliph al-Mansur, then in his eighth year in power, directly: you are a bad Muslim, more guilty than the Umayyad caliph Marwān whom you overthrew, and those descendants of the Prophet who rose up are better suited to rule than you. After writing this poem he lived another twenty years. There are accounts that he later altered the verses to turn their edge against al-Mansur's enemies. This shows that the newborn Abbasid monarchy, though a total state, was still a "new, soft" state, and the first generation of writers enjoyed a great deal of political freedom.

points.h: Insulting someone by declaring you won't insult them
points.body: Eighth-century Arabic satire often used a rhetorical device called apophasis (paralepsis): saying a thing by declaring that you will not say it. Bashshar used it against members of the Abbasid royal family — first advising his target to "seek my satisfaction, do not provoke me, a weak and decrepit man cannot bear the burden I lay on him," then offering fake praise: "how noble this man of Quraysh is, we do not deny his kinship with the Prophet, even if his mother is of low birth," then driving the knife in: his ancestors were lions of the tribe when they went to the evening feast, and jackals before the enemy. Bashshar compared his poetry to a branding iron searing into the other man's flesh.

points.h: Panegyric was a meal ticket, and also art
points.body: Beeston pointed out back in 1977: Abbasid poets sang the praises of the fabulously wealthy nobles who occasionally fought on the Byzantine frontier, and those lists of exaggerated courage and generosity "had little basis in reality" — writing panegyric was mostly about squeezing money out of the person being praised, and if the reward fell short of expectations, the poet turned around and wrote satire. But the host adds another layer: panegyric was both a calculated transaction and, at the same time, genuine gratitude and superb art. Early Abbasid society was astonishingly tolerant of political dissent — even satire aimed at the caliph and his family could exist; and the other side revealed by panegyric is that the Islamic cities along the Tigris and Euphrates were packed with the newly rich, and the private relationships between poets and patrons, based on appreciation of art, grew into the cross-cultural market of the later Islamic Golden Age — because the Golden Age really did need gold in the literal sense.

points.h: Poetry was the empire's pressure valve
points.body: The scholar Salma Jayyusi wrote that early Muslim society was full of tensions: a new hierarchy was emerging, different from the old tribal order, and rapidly gaining status as a source of power and wealth; society was moving steadily toward a more urban way of life; and a Bedouin people, suddenly thrown by conquest into a completely different world, produced a kind of anxiety — it took more than four generations of Islamization and urbanization to erase the influence of the pre-Islamic Arab way of life. From this the host concludes: eighth-century Islamic civilization was uneasy, and the new power relations left whole swathes of social groups feeling dispossessed. But in a city like Basrah, poetry and literature were the pressure valve — as a young man Bashshar watched the previous generation of poets, Jarir and al-Farazdaq, hurl coarse and hilarious verses at each other, and laughed along with the crowd until he could not stop; when he grew up he discovered that although certain strata of Arab society were closed to him, the Arabic language was public property for anyone with talent.
